name: Binary Search and Its Traps
intent: Use halving correctly: write the loop from an invariant instead of from memory, avoid the off-by-one hang and the midpoint overflow, find the first or last copy of a duplicated value, and notice that the same idea searches an answer space where no array exists.
scenario: A service looks up one value in a sorted list of 1,000,000 items. A scan can need 1,000,000 probes and halving needs 20, so the team writes a binary search. It passes every test, then hangs on a customer's data, returns the wrong copy of a duplicated timestamp, and in a different language fails on a very large range with a negative index.
problem: Binary search is easy to describe and famously easy to get wrong. The loop has several places where a one-off mistake does not crash but either hangs, skips a candidate or reads outside the range, and these bugs often show up only for particular positions of the target or particular sizes. The textbook version also answers a weaker question than people assume: it finds a match, not the first match. And the idea reaches further than arrays: any yes/no question that flips exactly once as a number grows can be searched by halving.

howItWorks.title: Halve a range that must contain the answer
howItWorks.text: Binary search keeps a range of positions that could hold the target and throws away half of it with each probe: look at the middle item, and if it is too small the target can only be to the right, otherwise it is not to the right. Every probe halves the range, so a list of n items needs at most about log2 n probes: 20 for 1,000,000 items, against up to 1,000,000 for a scan. A thousand times more items cost only about ten more probes. The price is that the list must already be sorted, and that you can jump to the middle in constant time, which an array allows and a linked list does not.

howItWorks.title: Write the loop from an invariant, not from memory
howItWorks.text: Most off-by-one errors vanish once you say in words what the range means and keep that promise. For example: the target, if present, is at a position in the half-open range lo up to but not including hi. Then start with lo = 0 and hi = n, loop while lo < hi, and each branch must keep the promise and shrink the range: if the middle item is too small, lo = mid + 1 (mid itself is ruled out); otherwise hi = mid (mid is still possible). Writing lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 breaks the shrink: when lo and hi are neighbours, mid equals lo and nothing changes, so the loop never ends. In the model, that version finds the first item fine and hangs on 3 of the 4 targets at every size we ran, which is why it survives a quick test.

howItWorks.title: Duplicates: decide which copy you mean
howItWorks.text: The textbook loop stops at the first probe that hits the target, so with duplicates it returns whichever copy the probes land on: with every value stored 4 times in 1,000 items, searching for the very first value returns index 2, not index 0. If you need the first copy, keep halving after a hit: the lower-bound form finds the first position whose value is not smaller than the target (11 probes here), then checks it. The last copy is the same search for the first position whose value is greater than the target, minus one. Counting copies is two such searches. The cost is one probe or so more than the any-match version, and the answer is the same every time.

howItWorks.title: The midpoint can overflow
howItWorks.text: (lo + hi) / 2 is correct on paper and wrong in a 32-bit signed integer once lo + hi passes 2,147,483,647: with lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 the sum wraps to -794,967,296 and the midpoint becomes -397,483,648, below the range. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 never exceeds hi, so it never overflows. This was found in the standard library's binary search of a major language years after it was written, because it needs a range of about a billion items to show. It is a language issue: JavaScript numbers are doubles and Python integers have no fixed width, so only the languages with fixed-width integers (C, C++, Java, C#, Go and others) are affected.

howItWorks.title: Search an answer space, not an array
howItWorks.text: Binary search needs a yes/no test that is false for small values and true for large ones, and flips once. Then you can search the numbers themselves without storing them. Example: the smallest ship capacity that moves 1,000 packages, in order, in 3 days. Testing one capacity costs one pass over the packages, and a bigger ship never does worse, so the answer is a threshold. Halving between the heaviest package (20) and the total (10,500) needs 13 checks, 13,000 steps; counting up from 20 needs 3,484 checks, 3,484,000 steps. The same pattern finds a square root, the smallest rate limit that passes a test, or the first bad commit in a history. The cost is the number of probes times the cost of one test.

pros: About log2 n probes: 20 for 1,000,000 items and 30 for a billion
Needs no extra memory: the loop keeps two numbers
Extends past arrays to any monotone yes/no question, such as a threshold or the first failing version
With an invariant written down, the code is short and checkable
cons: Needs sorted data and constant-time access to the middle, so it is wrong for a linked list or an unsorted list
Keeping the list sorted has a cost: each insert into a sorted array moves about n/2 items
Several one-off mistakes hang or misread the range without crashing, and tests that only try a few targets miss them
The textbook form finds any match, not the first or last, which matters as soon as values repeat
whenToUse: Many lookups against data that is sorted already or sorted once and then barely changes
Finding the first or last position of a value, or the boundary where a condition flips (a lower or upper bound)
Finding a threshold value when each candidate can be tested but the answers are not stored
whenNotToUse: A handful of lookups on a list that is not sorted: scanning is cheaper than sorting first (see sorting and searching complexity)
Very small lists, where a scan is as fast and simpler to get right
Data that changes constantly, where a hash table or a balanced tree serves lookups without keeping an array sorted
A condition that does not flip once as the number grows: halving then discards the answer
pitfalls: Writing lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 (or hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 in the closed-range form): the loop hangs when the range is two items wide, and only for some targets: in the model it works for the first item and gets stuck on the last, middle and missing ones, so a test with a single easy target passes

Mixing the two range conventions: a closed range (lo and hi both possible, loop while lo <= hi, hi = mid - 1) and a half-open one (hi excluded, loop while lo < hi, hi = mid) are each correct, but a mix of the two skips an item or never ends; pick one and write the invariant in a comment
Computing the midpoint as (lo + hi) / 2 in a fixed-width integer: with lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 the sum is -794,967,296 in 32 bits; use lo + (hi - lo) / 2

Assuming the match is the first one: with duplicates the any-match loop returns an arbitrary copy (index 2 of 4 equal values at the start of the list), so a lookup by timestamp can return a different row than a scan would; use a lower-bound search and say so in the function name

Searching data that is not sorted, or sorted by a different rule than the comparison uses: sorting strings by locale in the database and comparing them by code point in the code makes the 'sorted' promise false, and halving then misses items that are present

Searching an answer space with a test that is not monotone: if a smaller capacity works and a larger one does not, halving cannot find the threshold; check that a bigger value never does worse before trusting the search

Setting the answer range too tight or too loose: starting below the heaviest package returns a capacity that cannot carry it, and a huge upper bound costs only log2 more probes, so be generous rather than clever

Binary searching a list that is sorted descending with an ascending comparison, or comparing floating-point values containing NaN: the comparison is no longer a consistent order, and the result is wrong without any error

roles.description: Items in order, possibly with repeated values.

roles.description: The lo and hi that must still contain the answer.

roles.description: The comparison or condition that rules out half of the range.

roles.label: Answer
roles.description: The position, or the smallest value that passes the test.

quiz.question: A binary search is written with lo = mid in the branch that moves lo up. It works when the target is the first item but hangs on other targets. Why?
options: The list is not sorted, so the halving discards the wrong side.
When lo and hi are neighbours, mid equals lo, so the range stops shrinking.
The probe count goes over log2 n, which makes the loop run out of memory.
The midpoint is computed as a fraction, which is rounded to the same index.
quiz.explanation: With neighbours lo and lo + 1, the middle rounds down to lo, so lo = mid leaves the range unchanged and the loop repeats forever. Moving up needs lo = mid + 1, because mid itself has already been ruled out. Going left works because hi = mid does shrink the range, which is why a test on the first item passes.

quiz.question: A sorted list holds each value four times. The textbook binary search for a value that occurs at indexes 0 to 3 returns index 2. Which change makes it always return index 0?
options: Search a copy of the list sorted in descending order.
Use a larger step so the middle probe lands on the left edge.
Keep halving after a hit: find the first position whose value is not smaller than the target.
Run the same search twice and take the smaller of the two results.
quiz.explanation: The any-match loop stops at the first probe that hits, and which copy that is depends on the probes. A lower-bound search never stops at a hit: it keeps moving hi down until the range holds only the first position that is not smaller than the target, so the answer is the same every time.

quiz.question: Why is lo + (hi - lo) / 2 preferred to (lo + hi) / 2 in Java or C#?
options: It makes one fewer probe on lists with an odd number of items.
It rounds toward the first copy, which helps with duplicate values.
It avoids the division, which is slower than a subtraction.
lo + hi can exceed the largest 32-bit integer and wrap to a negative number.
quiz.explanation: With lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 the sum wraps to -794,967,296 and the midpoint is negative. hi - lo is never larger than hi, so lo + (hi - lo) / 2 stays in range. It gives the same midpoint otherwise: the probe count and the duplicate behaviour do not change.
